newsitem.title: USA: Coffee, soy, oil prices soar while copper falls.
newsitem.headline: Coffee, soy, oil prices soar while copper falls.

text.p: Coffee prices continued to surge Wednesday as speculators stormed the market on worries that crop problems will cut supplies later this year.

At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, March delivery coffee closed 5.10 cents higher at 144.60 cents a pound -- up 40 percent from its close on Dec. 6. March set a life-of-contract high at 147.80 cents earlier in the session.

Prices have soared in the last two months as evidence of tight stocks at coffee roasters emerged and news of smaller crops in Central American producers like Mexico and Nicaragua hit the market. Coffee officials in Mexico said last week dryness and freezes may cut Mexico's crop by 20 percent, or as much as one million 132-pound bags.

Estimates that Brazil's big crop would also be down 20 percent later this year and problems from a strike by port workers and truckers in No. 2 grower Colombia have also fuelled buying. News Monday of torrential rains in Colombia possibly damaging the crop only fed the fire.
"There have been heavy rains in Colombia and there are still concerns about the Brazil crop," said Merrill Lynch coffee analyst Judith Ganes.

Normally, an increased flow of newly harvested, high quality "arabica" beans from Latin America during the first quarter of the year builds stockpiles, but inventories have hovered at their lowest levels in some 20 years.
"Expectations had been new supplies would be coming in and they haven't," Ganes said. "Whatever has come in has been readily absorbed."

At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybeans led grain markets higher on talk the South American harvest would be delayed by rains. Such delays could prompt foreign buying of futures to lock in a delivery price for soybeans.
March soybeans ended 5-1/2 cents a bushel higher at $7.50 and March soybean meal rose a strong $3.50 per ton at $240.40.
"Some were talking about it being too wet in some areas (in northern Brazilian soybean areas) and not being able to harvest," said Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co.

Traders also continued to talk about dry weather in southern Brazilian fields that might lower soybean yields. A heavy pace of soybean crushing by domestic mills was also an underlying factor supporting soybeans and meal.

The speculative buying spilled over and March corn closed 1/4 cent a bushel higher at $2.75. But buying was capped by concerns that U.S. corn is being priced too high compared to Argentine supplies, traders said.
Lower prices from wheat exporters like Australia pushed down wheat prices, with traders keeping a sharp eye on pending results of a tender by India to buy at least 50,000 metric tons of wheat.
March wheat fell 2-3/4 cents a bushel to end at $3.70-1/4.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices rose sharply on cold weather forecasts as well as political tensions in Iraq. February heating oil closed 2.01 cents a gallon higher at 68.84 cents a gallon.

"It was a real mixed bag of things. There was news Saddam Hussein put his wife under house arrest, you are two days before (February contract) expiration, and it's a bit chilly out there," said trader Mike DeLuca of Prudential Securities.
March crude oil closed 57 cents higher at $24.47 a barrel and March gasoline rose 1.19 cents at 68.23 cents a gallon.
White House press secretary Mike McCurry, commenting on reports that Saddam had imprisoned his wife, said the White House sees "struggles for power" going on in Iraq.
On Tuesday a U.S. military official also said Saddam's military had increased training in recent weeks but there was no indication Iraq might repeat an attack on Kuwait.
Such an attack prompted the smashing of Saddam's forces by a U.S.-led military coalition in the 1991 Gulf War.

Copper prices ended sharply lower when the London Metal Exchange warned it was monitoring closely how price spreads between the LME and the New York market evolved. COMEX March copper closed 3.65 cents lower at 102.50 cents per pound.
"The mood has changed very quickly, with a lot of long liquidation now going on," Richard Hirsch of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said.

Traders said the drop Wednesday was too swift to see yet if consumers will now come in to buy and support the market. The first quarter of the year is normally the time of heaviest demand in the United States, and the physical market is still healthy and fairly tight, they said.
Producer ASARCO Inc., announcing its fourth quarter results Wednesday, said copper supply and demand were in balance and inventories at their lowest levels since mid-1990.
"At the same time, these favourable fundamentals appear to be replacing speculation as the primary influence in the copper market," ASARCO's Chairman Richard de J Osborne said.
